answer: CBA converted best. It is the only one of the three where the pre-provision (top-line) measure and the preferred bottom-line measure both grew, and the bottom line grew faster than the top line: operating performance (cash basis) rose 3% to $15,469m while cash NPAT rose 4% to $10,252m, a +~1pt positive conversion spread. Westpac converted second-best but from a declining base: pre-provision profit ex-Notable Items fell 3% to $10.5bn while net profit ex-Notable Items fell only 2% to $6,972m, also a +~1pt spread, but both legs were negative. NAB converted worst: underlying profit grew 1.3% to $10,965m, yet cash earnings fell 0.2% to $7,091m, a swing of roughly -1.5pt that reversed the sign of the result. The common swing factor below the pre-provision line was the direction of the credit impairment charge, not tax or minority interests (both minor for CBA/Westpac). CBA's loan impairment expense fell 9% ($76m), Westpac's fell 21% (7bps to 5bps of average loans), while NAB's rose 14.4% to $833m on individually assessed business-lending charges, compounded by a near-doubling of the minority-interest deduction. At the pre-provision line itself, CBA and NAB both grew because revenue-dollar growth outpaced expense-dollar growth despite mildly negative jaws in percentage terms (CBA income +5%/expenses +6%; NAB income +2.9%/expenses +4.6%), while Westpac's pre-provision profit fell outright because expense growth (+9%, including a $273m restructuring charge) far outpaced revenue growth (+3%) - a cost problem distinct from NAB's below-the-line credit problem. The three measures are not directly comparable: CBA's fiscal year ends 30 June 2025 versus 30 September 2025 for NAB and Westpac; CBA's cash-basis pre-provision figure still includes a $130m FY25 remediation/restructuring charge and NAB's underlying profit/cash earnings retain its own $130m payroll remediation charge, whereas Westpac's 'Notable Items' cover only hedging items and explicitly exclude its $273m restructuring charge; CBA and NAB separately disclose small discontinued-operations effects that Westpac does not split out; and minority interests are material only for NAB. The filings do not reveal FTE-level cost detail or the judgement quality behind each bank's impairment provisioning.

limitations: The three 'preferred earnings' measures (CBA cash NPAT, NAB cash earnings, Westpac net profit excluding Notable Items) are built from differently scoped exclusions, so growth-rate comparisons are directionally informative but not a strict apples-to-apples measure of underlying performance.
CBA's fiscal year ends 30 June 2025 and NAB/Westpac's end 30 September 2025, so 'FY25' covers non-identical 12-month windows and rate/macro backdrops.
The disclosures do not provide FTE-level or unit-cost detail behind expense growth, so the analysis cannot fully separate volume-driven cost growth from discretionary investment spend.
The disclosures do not reveal the underlying credit-quality judgement (e.g., concentration or recoverability of NAB's individually assessed charges) beyond the aggregate dollar figures given.

Discontinued-operations treatment differs (CBA and NAB break it out; Westpac's results as presented do not), which could marginally affect like-for-like comparison of the headline cash/core earnings growth rates.
This note does not estimate or infer any figure not printed in the source documents.
